description:
Sabbath rest is presented as serving several purposes that continue beyond its old-covenant sign function. Wesam Saad accepts that the Sabbath marked Israel’s covenant, but argues that this does not exhaust its meaning. He describes rest as trust in God the creator and provider, remembrance of deliverance, anticipation of future rest, and a day of delight and refreshment in God. Isaiah’s call to honour the day becomes central to his account of setting ordinary pursuits aside for direct communion with God. He also clarifies that this emphasis does not exclude personal devotion or faithful service during the rest of the week.

The second half answers the objection that the command disappears from the New Testament. Saad connects the Sabbath belonging to the Lord, Jesus’ lordship of it, and John’s reference to the Lord’s Day. He then compares the gathered worship, teaching, remembrance and covenant significance associated with the old and new settings. Communion and the resurrection shape his account of the church’s weekly assembly. He argues that finding ultimate rest in Christ does not itself cancel that pattern. The recording ends by announcing a further session on practical observance; questions about family time, provision and necessary activity are left unresolved here.

questions.question: Why does the Sabbath’s role as a covenant sign not exhaust its purpose?
questions.answer: Saad accepts the Exodus description of the Sabbath as a sign for Israel. He argues, however, that other passages give additional reasons for observance. Its covenant-sign function must therefore be considered alongside creation, provision, redemption, future rest and delight in God, rather than treated as the only explanation.

questions.question: How is rest connected with God’s provision?
questions.answer: Saad presents stepping back from ordinary income-producing work as a practical expression of trust in God as creator and provider. The day is not described simply as inactivity, but as time dedicated to worship. This is one purpose within his broader theological account of rest, rather than the whole argument.

questions.question: How does remembrance of deliverance lead to Christ?
questions.answer: The teacher begins with Israel’s rescue from slavery in Egypt and then traces a pattern of redemption culminating in Christ. He connects the serpent conflict and the Exodus story with deliverance from the power of darkness. These connections are presented as his reading of the redemptive pattern, not as a replacement of the historical Exodus account.

questions.question: What future rest is distinguished from believers’ present rest in Christ?
questions.answer: Saad acknowledges present spiritual rest through forgiveness while pointing to rest still to come beyond the struggle of this life. He draws on Hebrews and Revelation to describe that hope and the end of labour. The weekly pattern is therefore presented as looking forward as well as remembering past deliverance.

questions.question: What does it mean to call the Sabbath a delight?
questions.answer: In Saad’s exposition of Isaiah, ordinary pursuits are set aside so that God himself becomes the direct object of delight. He describes this as refreshment and renewed communion, rather than the denial of all pleasure. The distinction is between seeking the usual sources of satisfaction and deliberately delighting in the Lord.

questions.question: Does the weekly emphasis mean devotion and service matter only on one day?
questions.answer: No. Saad expressly affirms personal devotion on other days and receiving from God through faithful work and family responsibilities. He distinguishes those regular duties from a day devoted to direct communion within the gathered church. The emphasis on one day is not presented as permission to neglect God during the rest of the week.

questions.question: How does Saad connect the Sabbath with the Lord’s Day?
questions.answer: He brings together the day belonging to Yahweh, Jesus’ claim to be Lord of the Sabbath, and John’s reference to the Lord’s Day. Saad reads these expressions as continuity in the day’s meaning, with the weekday question addressed in the preceding session. He takes John’s expression to refer to Sunday, while explaining that the connection concerns more than a change in terminology.

questions.question: What similarities does he draw between the earlier Sabbath assembly and the church’s gathering?
questions.answer: He compares regular assembly, instruction, remembrance of redemption and covenant significance. Acts and Corinthians are used in his argument for weekly gathered worship and communion, while the church’s relationship to Christ gives the gathering its New Testament emphasis. He also stresses the church as the gathered body, giving this practice a distinctive place in New Testament life.

questions.question: Why does ultimate rest in Christ not cancel weekly observance in his argument?
questions.answer: Saad rejects that conclusion by comparison with marriage: its reference to Christ and the church does not make human marriage obsolete. He uses the analogy to argue that spiritual fulfilment in Christ does not, by itself, remove the continuing practice being discussed. Detailed application of that practice is still reserved for the announced next session.
